utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Madam Registrar, could you call the indicates, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Oric, good morning to you. Can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I can indeed follow the proceedings in my own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Oric. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours I'm Patricia Sellers for the Office of the Prosecutor. With us today are co-counsel Mr. Gramsci di Fazio, Ms. Joanne Richardson and our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink. And good morning to the Defence also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Sellers and good morning to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Vasvija Vidovic. Together with Mr. John Jones, I represent Mr. Naser Oric. And we are joined by our legal assistant, Ms. Jasmina Cosic, and our case manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts. And good morning to the Prosecution as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Vidovic and good morning to you and your team. Let me start with a few good and bad news. It's start with the good news. I spoke with Judge Eser yesterday and he expects to be with us on Monday. Of course, it's not 100 per cent. If it does not happen, then according to the -- we cannot continue to sit under Rule 15 bis(A) which allows us to sit today. So I'm being clear about that. So that's number 1. But he expects -- I spoke to him yesterday and he expects to be here. The situation is a little bit better, lass improved. The other thing, you will recall that two days ago, when we had that technical hitch, and during which we were supposedly in private session and we were discussing -- or I was rather raising my concern to the fact that the Prosecution had not yet responded to a motion, which you filed confidentially pursuant to Rule 70, we agreed that -- after we resumed, after the technical hitch, that we didn't have -- need to have what we discussed informally at the time because it was not being formally transcribed, we didn't need to have it in transcript, et cetera, and that I would raise the matter the next sitting which was yesterday. And of course, yesterday we started, we had a long and difficult morning, and we did not deal with the matter so I'm dealing with the matter today. First of all I wish to inform you that if you insist that what was discussed two days ago informally in the records, you want it in the transcript, we can have it in the transcript even though it does not exist in the English version because it exists in the French version. So there is a French version of it. If you're interested we have -- we can have it translated. However, what my suggestion is, to go in private session for a couple of minutes now, we deal with it, Ms. Sellers will update us on the situation, and then we will decide what to do. If you are agreeable to this. I see the Defence nodding. I see the Prosecution nodding so let's go into private session for a couple of minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The other thing which literally took me a little bit by surprise this morning, although I knew that it was in the offing, particularly with regard to Courtroom III is that construction work is scheduled for the three court rooms at different times, of course, but partly overlapping. To be precise, part -- the latter part of the reconstruction work for Courtroom I will overlap with the first part of the construction work for Courtroom III and the last part required for the reconstruction of Courtroom II would overlap with the first part needed for the reconstruction of Courtroom I. We are talking of a space that starts of a period of time that starts from November and right through the end of February. Courtroom II will be affected it seems during the months of November and December. Courtroom I, it seems, will be affected during the months of December and January. That's where the least harm is done. And Courtroom III will be affected during the months of January and February. Now, I am also told by way of comfort, which I am relaying that, that while this work is going on, first of all, the Court -- the relative courtrooms will not be available. In other words, while -- for example, Courtroom II is undergoing construction, it will be, I am told, completely closed for trial purposes. Courtroom I, you know, is busy every morning or most mornings with one particular case. So although I am assured that every attention is being taken and plans are underway to obstruct the least possible this, the smooth planning and progress of cases. I am pretty sure that our case, like other cases, will probably be to an extent affected. We will definitely have to move, I'm preparing you for this, from courtroom to courtroom but that is no big deal. We've done it in the past and it wouldn't worry me in the least, but I think there may be -- don't consider it a problem, but there may be problems on the way. I promise you that I will, together with my two colleagues, do our level best to secure courtroom space as much as possible, not to delay the case any further, and because of there of course I will keep you informed as we go along. But it is bound to cause some problems. It is bound to cause some problems. I'll try to make sure as much as possible beforehand that we know the exact dates when we will not be sitting, if at all, so that you would know and you would ensure that you don't bring witnesses here for nothing. So it's -- just came to my desk this morning and I will be discussing it -- doesn't depend much on us but in so far as it depends on us we will do our utmost but we will discuss it with the authorities here to see what can be done to avoid undesired stoppages, but these works have to be undertaken. It's not something which is being capriciously done because all the courtrooms need to be enlarged to extend their capacity, particularly in view of joinders that are taking place and may take place as well. So, of course, we understand the situation. Next thing is, before we bring in the witness, I would like to know whether you have any preliminaries.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no preliminaries but just arising out of your last comment, this morning we did receive a schedule, I believe, on the remaining court days and I just want to know at this point in time should we use this as the basis that will be modified or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This is -- this was obviously prepared without consideration being given to the fact that between, for example, December and -- November and December, Courtroom II will be unavailable, and, as you know, we mostly work in Courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I don't know what to tell you, Ms. Sellers, but the thing is I will take it up with the authorities without much delay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: We appreciate that very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Immediately. And I promise you I'll do my very best. I have got every interest to see this case come to an end, as -- you know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, no other preliminaries for our part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So what you have received is sitting days will definitely be subject to some alterations as we go ahead, and I will try to give you prior notice, sufficient notice of the time, I mean. Yes any preliminaries on your side?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Richardson, before -- you can bring in the witness in the meantime. Please keep in your mind, take consideration what we went through yesterday and if I tell you to stop and we have a break, please try to cooperate as much as you can.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, good morning to Your Honours. I will keep yesterday in mind and allow for breaks as well as look to Your Honour for directions on that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Kolenovic, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome back. You see we are sitting in a much bigger courtroom this morning. We have more space. You don't need to repeat the solemn declaration that you made yesterday. It still applies today. So I invite you to make yourself comfortable straight away, and I hope you've had time to unwind a little bit and rest and that you are fresh now and prepared for the cross-examination that Ms. Richardson from the Prosecution bench will be proceeding with very shortly. Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, before we get started perhaps I could have the usher's assistance in lowering the ELMO a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Or moving it backwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Moving it back. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it well placed now Ms. Richardson?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you very much. Thank you to the usher as well. Cross-examined by Ms. Richardson:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Kolenovic. As Your Honour indicated my name is Joanne Richardson and I'm a lawyer with the Prosecution. This morning I will have a series of questions for you clarifying some information that you gave yesterday about your experiences in Srebrenica. If for any reason you do not understand my question, I would ask you to indicate that if we are unclear about the dates, please inform me so that I will either rephrase the question or we will pinpoint what date I'm referring to. Also, if you would keep your answers as brief as possible, it's my intention to get through your testimony today. Of course, if you need to expound on your answer and give us additional information, feel free to do so as well. I would first like to start off by asking you about Srebrenica. I believe you said you lived in Srebrenica all of your life; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were born there, you went to school there?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your husband, Ramic, is that correct, his first name?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is his first name?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ramiz, with a Z.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I thank you very much and if I don't pronounce anyone else's name correctly this morning, please feel free to correct me. Was your husband also born in Srebrenica and did he go to school there as well?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was he born?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was born in Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you married in Srebrenica as well?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did your husband move to Srebrenica, if you know?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your children were born in Srebrenica, I take it?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not both of them. My youngest son was born in Srebrenica, Elvis, and the second one, that is to say the eldest, was born in Serbia, in a place called Dubova [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to ask you about what you did prior to the war, prior to the outbreak in 1992. I believe you testified that you were working for a company; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do for them?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the accounting service. I worked as an accountant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. And your husband, what did he do prior to the outbreak of the war?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was an electrician.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it you -- both you and your husband had family members living in Srebrenica, is that -- would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's talk about some of your family members. Your parents live there?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you have brothers, sisters, cousins, nephews, in laws, as well?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't have any brothers?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had brothers and sisters, and a big family, and -- but I did not have anyone on my husband's side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying that. Clearly, I asked one question too many. So how many brothers did you have and how many sisters did you have?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two sisters and a brother.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was your family members in Srebrenica during the war?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My mother and my father were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your brother was not, or your sister?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just to be clear, your husband did not have any relatives in Srebrenica during the time of the war, or before?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, with respect to your extended family, if you had one, did you have cousins that resided in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the war? I don't understand the question. Could you please repeat it? You mean during the war?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Any uncles or aunts who resided in Srebrenica during the war?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us how many uncles did you have that resided in Srebrenica during the war? That's the period that I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had two aunts, an uncle, and then this uncle had a son, another uncle had a son, also an uncle's sister, aunts, their sons. I had a lot of relatives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you tell us -- just give us a general idea about the ages of the relatives that you had? Were they elderly to very young? Did their ages vary?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were both old and young.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to ask you about some of the residents in Srebrenica since you've lived there for a very long time, all of your life. In particular, I'd ask if you know Ramiz Beserovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I want to make sure that she has understood. I wasn't following in B/C/S. I'm following in English, of course, but you mean Becirevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Becirevic. Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it Ramiz or Ramis.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: It's Ramiz.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: With a Z. Ramiz.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I knew Ramiz Becirevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did he do prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe he was at the staff or in the municipal office. I saw him around. I don't know exactly what job he was doing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during the war, did you see him in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... where he was at the times that you saw him?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the post office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Hakija Meholjic?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Meholjic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you familiar with him as well?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was my neighbour at the place where I was born in Petrica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you have occasion to see him during the war?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was he?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the Domavija hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned seeing Mr. Becirevic at the post office. Is that also referred to as the PTT building?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you familiar with what Mr. Halilovic did prior to the war? Meholjic, excuse me, Meholjic, thank you.

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was a police officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with Akif Ustic?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's a distant relative.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did he do prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a physical education teacher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, some of the other individuals I'd like to ask you about, I guess first I should ask you whether you are familiar with others who lived not only in the town of Srebrenica but in the surrounding villages as well. Do you know some of those individuals? Were you familiar with them?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some who had come to live in Srebrenica and who built houses there. In peace time, I never went to any of the villages. I didn't even know that there were so many villages around Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you familiar with -- either prior -- this individual that I'm about to ask you about, either prior to or during the war, Mirzet Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know him -- did you know him before the war?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did he do prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. He's a relative but I really don't know. We didn't really visit each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him in Srebrenica during the war?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once, in passing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you saw him, where was he?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know if he had any particular responsibility in Srebrenica during the war?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you also familiar with Osman Osmanovic?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when I ask were you familiar with him, if either during the war or before. So you didn't -- you've never met him at either periods?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know who Osman Osmanovic is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I believe you mentioned Akif Ustic, that he's a distant relative and that he was a physical education teacher before the war, correct?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during the war, did you happen to meet him on any occasion?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So during all of 1992, you didn't see him at all?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your husband know Akif Ustic?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He knew him but he didn't see him during the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How is it that you know that?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know he never said anything, only when Akif was killed, he told me that Akif was killed. This was information that spread quickly through the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know if he also knew Mr. Meholjic?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did your husband see him during the war?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your husband tell you what the circumstances were when he would see Mr. Meholjic?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you how often he saw him?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can just explain it like this. When my brother-in-law, my sister's husband, came to Srebrenica, when Nurif came with the soldiers, then my brother-in-law, who lived in Bratunac before the war with my sister, came from Tuzla to Srebrenica, they brought medicines, and my brother-in-law was in the unit, in Hakija Meholjic's unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you just tell me the name of -- the full name of your brother-in-law again?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bekir Smajlovic from Bratunac. He was killed in 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with Hamid Salilovic?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps Hamid Salihovic. That's a last name that you have in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That's exactly who I was referring to. Did you know him prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know him during the war?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of Zulfo Tursunovic?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you know of Mr. Tursunovic?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war, I knew that he had -- I don't know, in a cafe or something, something happened, and he was convicted for that, and that's how I knew him before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him during the war?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps a couple of times, just in passing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what role, if any, did he play in Srebrenica during the war?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Everybody was talking about it, that he was a commander or something. I don't really understand these military things so I really wouldn't -- I don't know. I wasn't interested in that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. Well, did your husband ever talk about Zulfo Tursunovic, meeting with him or talk about him in any other capacity?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also, I would ask if you know Naser Oric. And this is before the war specifically.

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the war, did you meet him or come to know of him?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard of him, and I met him just once.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you meet him?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was in the hospital, when there were a lot of killed and wounded and when my brother-in-law was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you tell us about the circumstances of the meeting? Did you have a conversation with him?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was he doing when you saw him at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were thousands, several thousand people around the hospital. Everybody will come to see who had been wounded, and I was there. I was helping in the hospital. All of us civilians, women, girls, were there helping. There were a lot of people who were wounded and they were lying around the hospital, as far as the post office, and that's how I knew Naser. It was just that one meeting. It was like this. Somebody was crying a lot and wailing and shouting and they were hitting their head at the -- against the hospital wall and I was asking who had been killed. That was close to this person and somebody said that that was Naser. I didn't really look that much. I just kind of glanced but somebody said it was Naser and that he was beating his head against the wall and he was wailing and shouting and crying because of all of the people that had been killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall after what action this took place, when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was in January, when my brother-in-law was killed, maybe in mid-January. I don't know exactly which date. I can't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But we are talking about 1993, correct?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall if you had gone searching for food around that time, either on that day or the day before?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was later, in January.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But I'm trying to determine exactly when it was that you saw Naser, and --

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In January 1993, mid-January. I don't know if it was the 17th, the 18th or the 15th of January. I really can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. Do you recall -- well, you testified that your brother-in-law had been killed. Is that correct? Was it around that time?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall what action your brother-in-law was involved in?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the lake, Jezero. I also went to Jezero, and then I returned because of the shelling. There were a lot of wounded and I came back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your husband also involved in this action at Jezero?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My husband was there. My husband went everywhere where you could find any food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, getting back to what you know about -- what you knew or what you were told about Naser Oric, what was it exactly that you knew about him?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really didn't know anything much because I wasn't interested. The most important thing for me were my children, my family, my family. I never thought of myself first but of my children, my parents, my husband. That was the most important thing to me. I didn't have time to ask who was Zulfo, who was Naser, who was Hakija, what they were doing. I really wasn't interested in that at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I understand. When you were in the hospital, though, and the person said that that's Naser, what else did they say about him? Was he important, that this is why this person was pointing him out to you?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what they told me. Also about Zulfo. They also told me about Zulfo. I didn't know who Zulfo was. In passing, just by coincidence somebody would call out Zulfo, and then I knew. They were some kind of commanders. I don't know. I don't know how they were organised or anything like that. I really don't know. I really don't want you to -- I'm not some kind of military strategist here so that you would ask me about such details, key details. I'm only here because I want to tell the truth, and I don't want to say one single lie. As I said, for ten years I have been looking for missing persons and we have been proving the truth and we have been trying to secure the future for our country and for the coming generations in Srebrenica, from 1992, from day one, when the Serbs came, there was only death and catastrophe and nothing more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand perfectly that you're not a military expert. My question only has to do with what you were told, what you heard about Naser Oric or Zulfo Tursunovic so that the record is clear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it's a couple of matters. Firstly, the witness has been asked whether anything else was said apart from that it was Naser and I believe she's answered that that's what she was told, it was Naser and she wasn't told anything else. There is a more -- and so I would object to my learned friend persisting. If the witness's answer that that's all she heard that he was pointed out, and the same with Zulfo, and that she didn't know anything more, then she shouldn't persist with that line of questioning. More importantly, I've -- for the last sort of ten minutes from raising one point because it didn't particularly seem to be going anywhere but according to Rule 90(H)(i), cross-examination, of course, is limited to the subject matter of evidence-in-chief and matters affecting credibility. Of course, where the witness is able to give evidence relevant to the case for the cross-examining party, they can do so. But I don't understand that Rule to allow a fishing expedition where the Prosecution simply probes and asks just in the hope of getting some information from the witness which might be helpful. If there is actually something clear, a point which the Prosecution either want to put to the witness or something which we have a basis for trying to establish with the witness, that's one thing. But to simply, as I say, to go on a fishing expedition when I haven't in examination-in-chief mentioned Naser Oric or Zulfo Tursunovic or any of these people, just to probe endlessly in the hope the witness might mention something is not in my submission within the contemplation of Rule 90(H)(i). The Prosecution should have to say what, what are they trying to establish in this line of questioning. What actually are they after.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And clearly perhaps we need to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There mat hears arisen in the past when you were -- whether I say you, I mean, your -- the Defence. So I think it has been dealt with already. Yes. Ms. Richardson, let me hear what you have to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, certainly, Your Honour, the witness has testified that -- well, first --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Shall we keep the witness in or at one time at one time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I would ask that we have this discussion outside the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam, we need to discuss something for which you need not be present. So Madam Usher will escort you out of the courtroom for a few minutes. Stay within reach, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's put it like this. Let me hear you first, Ms. Richardson, and then I'll just explain what Rule 90, the relevant part of Rule 90 states.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I think my response will go directly to the relevance. The portion of the rule, section H(1) which speaks to giving evidence that is relevant to the case as it pertains to cross-examination, and I do believe that counsel, Defence counsel, cannot make the argument that trying to elicit from the witness the role of the Accused in Srebrenica at the time is not relevant. Not only that, Your Honour, during the examination-in-chief, counsel examined the witness as to what was going on in Srebrenica at the time and I think that certainly we need to determine exactly who the players were in Srebrenica. And my line of questioning has to do with exactly what the witness knew about certain individuals, what she knew about actions which was raised by Defence counsel yesterday. And Defence counsel himself on prior occasions has said and I quote, as pertaining -- as it pertains to cross-examination, Mr. Jones stated on the 23rd of March, during his cross-examination of Mr. Bogilovic, he stated, "I will leave discreetly halfway through," and I'm quoting at this time. "Secondly I apologise if my intervention earlier was not welcome. It was really a problem. I felt should be made which is that there have been a -- there have been continuing objections by the Prosecution that matters were not raised during examination-in-chief. And I think it has to be said that it's crystal clear from Rule 90(H)(i) that we were not limited to only matters that have been raised in examination-in-chief. If there is evidence which relevant to the case for the cross-examining party then of course it can be cross-examined upon and indeed it would be absurd and unfair if the witness could give very helpful evidence to the Defence and he was not allowed to give that evidence because the Prosecution has not asked him about it." And so, Your Honour, we are back to the reverse situation where Mr. Jones has conducted his examination-in-chief, my cross-examination has to do with relevant and pertinent matters. It could be argued that these are the most relevant and pertinent matters in this case, one of them, in any event, and I think that this is clearly not a fishing expedition and this witness has valuable information to offer about Srebrenica and the individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you want to reply, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your honour, just briefly. Firstly as far as Rule 90(H)(i) is concerned I mentioned it at the outset today. I'm obviously not going to dispute the Rule 90(H)(i). It says what it says. Of course it does. On the previous occasion whether this came up, there were interruptions from the Prosecution that matters hadn't been raised in examination-in-chief and I quite properly pointed out that Rule 90(H)(1) says what it does, and when challenged on that occasion it was to do with I think Hazim from Voljavica and the look-alike, I think a look-alike to Naser Oric and we said that's plainly relevant and that was dealt with properly on that occasion. So I don't see what possible bearing what happened on that occasion has with today. As far as this matter is concerned, it's one thing to say -- and I'm glad the Prosecution spelt out why they are asking about Akif and Zulfo and the rest of it. But if it's to work out what the role, if any, of those persons were that's one thing they can put the matter to the witness. "Do you know what role, if any, these people had," and she can answer. In fact, she has answered very clearly, "I don't know anything about what their roles were, I'm not a military strategist, I don't know those details." In fact she has answered that question and we should probably move on in any event. But that's quite different from saying, "Did you ever hear of so and so, did you have a conversation with him, what did he say?" That clearly is a fishing expedition because it's hoping that perhaps the witness will let drop something. It's quite different from just saying "Do you know Akif Ustic, do you know what role if any he had in Srebrenica," yes, no, and then moving on. So I draw a distinction between those different ways of proceeding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are trying to be as brief as possible, so not to take time out of that which is required for the completion of the testimony of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just interrupt you just briefly so that I can add that, indeed, when I asked about various individuals and what roles they played, if any, this goes directly into what was asked in examination-in-chief about local authorities. So I have just simply presented a series of questions to determine who was there and what role, whether be it as authoritative figure or not that person may have played in Srebrenica. Not only is it part of the examination-in-chief, it's relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. The position as put forward by paragraph H of Rule 90 is clear. It does not give place for any interpretation, basically, because it's a clear piece of law. We've dealt with it in the past. As you know, cross-examination, as imported here, is not exactly the cross-examination that is standard everywhere because the rules vary from jurisdiction to jurisdiction. The position is as follows: That normally cross-examination should be limited to the subject matter of the evidence-in-chief, as we all know, and that's the essence of -- but also, as rightly pointed out by Mr. Jones to matters affecting the credibility of witnesses, and this, you establish as you go along and not beforehand. I would never know exactly why a question is being put, whether it's to test the credibility of a witness, until most of the time we have proceeded quite -- but also cross-examination is allowed where the witness is able to give evidence relevant to the case for the cross-examining party to the subject matter of the -- of that case. Now, this is explained in the next paragraph, subparagraph, and it is predicated, as you all know, on the assumption or on the established fact that there is a contradiction between the evidence given by the -- by the witness and the nature of the case that the examining counsel or cross-examining counsel is interested in. If this is the case, then there is only one requirement which we haven't -- we haven't so far come to that stage in this particular cross-examination. In that case, you need to put the witness on notice, and you need to explain to the witness the nature of the case which you consider to be in contradiction with the witness -- with what the witness would be testifying. Then there is the overriding, I would say, discretionary power of the Trial Chamber itself to allow enquiry into additional matters. Now, obviously we would intervene there if we hear an objection from your part and we will obviously need to know from the cross-examining counsel what is being sought from the witness, and then we will decide of course whether to allow additional inquiry into additional matters. Until now, I think although we may have chosen the -- a lengthy path to get to the answers or to the information that the Prosecution was seeking by the cross-examination, I think we are still there, and I don't think there is need for the Trial Chamber to intervene. What we are doing -- what we would like you to do is to cut short, if necessary, the route that you may -- you may envisage, that you need, in order to seek the information from the witness. I mean, you are in cross-examination and you can go really direct. So if you can do that, we will recuperate time and also try to possibly finish.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We do see the relevance of what you --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Indeed. Just so it's clear as this discussion is taking place outside of the witness it may appear as though I'm asking questions that are seemingly going no where. But in fact they are going somewhere and I just haven't gotten to that point yet. The series of questions I asked initially about what various people did for a living, well, the witness testified yesterday that all elicited by Mr. Jones that all of the educated persons in Srebrenica had left. So I saw it fit to inquire as to it who remained and what they did for a living. That goes directly to what was inquired about yesterday and certainly to whether or not it is the fact that the educated people left. So I'd ask the Bench to bear with me as I'm asking some of these questions that may seem at first glance to not have a purpose. But indeed, every question that I'm asking does have a purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And is relevant and probative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's your point of view and point taken, of course, but if we have an objection we will have to attend to that objection as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And if the objection is valid, of course we will ask you to move to another question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Indeed, indeed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So is it clear enough?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, both of you. Usher, could you please readmit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Kolenovic, and if I mispronounce your name, please correct me. I seem to have a heavy tongue this morning. Did your husband talk about Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you testified yesterday as well as this morning earlier that your husband -- I'll rephrase the question. During the period of time that you were in your apartment during that 20-day period that you talked about yesterday, when the Serbs were in Srebrenica, do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you testified that your husband was not with you at the time and in fact he was hiding in the woods. Do you recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He wasn't in the woods, in fact. He had gone to check on my parents, to Petrica, and my parents used to live at Petrica, and later on when he came back, he told me that they were forced to take to the woods to hide from the Serbs because the Serbs used to get into houses at Petrica. First of all, they took cars and then all the household appliances, and some people were even killed and three or four houses were set on fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, I do recall that testimony from yesterday. But during the time following -- I'll rephrase the question. At some point he went to the woods, along with all of the able-bodied men, I think you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't put it quite like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So did there come a point in time that he did go to the woods?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When he came back, when the whole family was reunited once again over that period, those 20-odd days, I don't know how precise I can be here, but together with the rest of the population that had stayed in Petrica, and together with my parents, he went to the woods. He didn't go with all those other men but with the population in general. The entire population that was in that street, I mean, I don't know who stayed behind because I was in another part of town. They all took to the woods nearby.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And --

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I meant. I don't know how you interpreted my statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. And I appreciate your clarifying that, but certainly they were in the woods, including the men who were not in their apartments, or not in their houses?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he mention the names of any other individuals that he was with, other than the general population?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was just the population, no one else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he -- did he mention whether Hakija Meholjic was there, or Akif Ustic?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We found out later that they were very close.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he mention Naser Oric as being among the people that he was with?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how to explain this to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine, thank you. Was your husband in a unit? When I mean a unit, such as you mentioned that your brother-in-law was in a unit. Was your husband in a unit as well?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And which unit was he in, do you know?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but I know that he was with somebody called Mido and I don't know his family name. I mean, I myself as a mother was primarily interested in other things and not that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. Did he mention anyone other than Mido as being in this unit?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember, but for example if someone was killed or wounded, he would give me the name of the person. But I didn't know all of them because there were quite a few people from other municipalities, new arrivals in my town, so I really didn't know them. I can say that I knew some people whom I've already mentioned such as Hakija Meholjic who was a neighbour, and some other neighbours over many years. I can say something about those people. But I saw them very rarely because there were huge numbers of refugees. So actually I didn't even come across the locals very often. My primary interest was sheer survival for myself and my children and how I could protect my children from shelling, from the killings and how I could get food. I didn't really have much spare time. I didn't have a split second in which to consider what anyone else was doing or where they were going or what they were up to. Nobody asked any questions or paid any heed to that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. And you stated that you didn't -- your house would mention to you when someone died and you didn't know everyone, that they were refugees. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And his unit was made up of -- and so his unit was made up of refugees, as well as men from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In that part of town where we were, there were not too many locals in the area, perhaps just a couple. Most of the people were refugees. Only in Petrici, most of the population were locals from Srebrenica, in the Petrici street for the most part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he ever mention to you how many men were in his unit?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't a unit as such. Everybody went looking for food like I did. I don't think we can consider it to be a unit or for it to be an army or something. I really can't talk much about that because I think somebody else would be a more appropriate person. Perhaps my husband could come and testify here. I'm here to tell the truth but I don't know about these things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just stop you for a moment. Is your husband alive, Ms. Kolenovic?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the former Yugoslavia, yes. He lives in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did he have -- your husband, that is, did he have a weapon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's be time specific, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1992, during the period of the war, did he have a weapon? 1992 and, of course, 1993.

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When he was in Bjelovac, he found a rifle, I don't know what rifle -- I don't know whether it was an automatic or some other rifle but he found it in a Serb house in Bjelovac, but I'm not into arms. Even before the war, I hated the sight of armed police officers, even though that's something you need in every country.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to that, did he have a weapon?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And did he bring this weapon home that he found in Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And other than this weapon, did he have any other weapons that you know of?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He found two big knives. They were very big, and they had blades on both sides, and he brought those weapons home, and I said to him, I hated the sight of those things in my house and that he should throw them out and get rid of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall when it was that he brought the knives home with him, where he got them?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he was in Bjelovac. It was in winter. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And other than your husband, and your brother-in-law, the other male relatives that you mention who were in Srebrenica, were they also part of a group of men who would go out and fight?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everyone went somewhere. As to whether they fought or whether they didn't, they all fought for their lives. I can't be very specific about this. I didn't really have any contact with my family at the time. I simply didn't have time. I didn't have time to go and visit my extended family. I just sometimes visited my parents and I had two sons and I needed to get food for them and my husband went looking for food as well. I had elderly parents and it was quite enough. I had enough on my plate as it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'd like to just change to another topic for a moment. The pictures that were shown to you yesterday, I'd like to show them to you and ask you a bit of -- ask you to give us a bit more information about what we saw in the pictures.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could have the usher's assistance in showing the witness photograph number 1, P725 [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Maybe we should say it's D725.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What did she say?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It says P the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see. Definitely that's wrong. It's D725.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Kolenovic, if you take a look at the photograph, I believe it's on Sanction as well, is that -- Ms. Kolenovic, if you look at the ELMO, at the photograph that you were shown yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I'm not sure -- oh, she is. Okay. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you first tell us who was it that gave you this photograph?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 10th anniversary of the events in Srebrenica was marked recently and, at Potocari, somebody gave a big album with those photos to my president and when I got to the association premises I found this on the desk. And they brought those photos along so that people could perhaps recognise someone on those photos. It was when General Morillon entered Srebrenica and when the doctors came in, and so one of them took those photos. Because we've got more. It's a big, fat album, and there are pictures of those people who had come in at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall what month it was -- and this is 1993, I assume, you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall what month it was that General Morillon came?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: April, perhaps. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you pointed out in the photograph your house, your apartment. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as you look --

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as you look at this photograph, do you recall whether looking at the scene in this photograph, such as, for instance, there is a truck here, you see that?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the truck has in it some debris? You see that? There seems to be an old car and other types of debris in it.

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps it's my car even, but I had seen a similar one in town later but it was green.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And there is a horse in the picture as well. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, first I'd like to ask you -- let's take the horse first. Were there many horses in Srebrenica during the war and leading up until the point when this picture was taken?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if there had been very many but there were horses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who owned them, do you know?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. I didn't understand what you meant. There were people and horses. I saw more people than horses, but -- could I perhaps clarify?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Absolutely, please.

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, that was because there were no means of transport, so people would build some kind of wooden structures or they would use the wheels off containers or smashed cars, and they made trolleys to carry wood or whatever. So actually they were drawing those trolleys or carriages, make shift carriages so it was the people that acted as horses. And as I said before, in spite of all the progress, having been made by the human civilisation at that point in time, we had been thrown back by 500 years by the Serbs. We didn't have anything for firewood. If I were to tell you that I wasted three to four house hours going from door-to-door.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop. Please restrict your answer to the question that was put to you. Don't give us more information. Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Ms. Kolenovic, is it correct that the people including yourself and others, the people who lived in Srebrenica, including the refugees, used whatever means they could as a form of transportation? In other words, apparatus that they constructed, acted themselves as horses, used cars, perhaps the wheels on the cars, to transport things?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there were also horses? Animal, itself?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were horses as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these were -- I'll withdraw that question. Now, let's talk about the truck for a moment. This truck appears to be operational. Do you recall if you saw this truck or other trucks in Srebrenica around this -- the time period that this photograph was taken?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So not only this truck but you may have seen other trucks as well?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only saw one truck, that Ramo Hljebara used to carry the wounded in. That is to say when they had fuel. If they had no fuel, they couldn't do that. So I saw that one truck that Ramo Hljebara was using to carry the wounded and that was it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It was just a clarification of the time frame because the first question referred to when the photograph was taken, so 93, and then the flex question so not only this truck but you may have seen other trucks as well, since it's time unspecific we are not sure what the answer is going to refer to.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please address this with a specific question, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Also, at there point, I think it's pertinent to know whether this truck that Madam has been describing to us is the same truck that we see in the photo or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Indeed. Indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just so that we are clear about your answer, the truck that you saw --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will need to have a break in two minutes or a few minutes' time any way.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I'll end on this topic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The truck that you saw Ramo carrying the wounded in, when -- what time period was this?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1993, when the UNPROFOR people came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see it in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Occasionally. Very rarely, because I was basically next door to the hospital. Very rarely. Perhaps if they could find some fuel, occasionally but it was very rarely. I can't tell you I did not see him because I did, but it was very rarely, perhaps some two or three occasions. I didn't count really. I can't be very precise about this. I mean, as to how many times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. Is this the same truck that you saw?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we can take a break now, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have a 25-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Kolenovic, before the break we were discussing the photographs and I'd like you to take a look at it again. I'm just seeking to elicit information about what we see in the photograph itself. We were talking about vehicles and you stated that this is not the vehicle that you saw in 1992 that belonged to the person you knew; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, that's not the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The truck.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I used to see the truck and that I used to see another vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, did you -- I see here in the photograph that there seems to be some clothing to the right of the photograph, that's -- appears to be clothes hung out to dry in the apartment building. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So now in the period that this picture was taken, which I believe you stated it was given to you and it was believed to have been taken following demilitarisation, during that period of time, you yourself and other residents in Srebrenica were able to wash your clothes, hang it out to dry, in other words have a sense of normalcy to life?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had to wash our clothes, what we had, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course. Perfectly understandable. Now, also in the photograph I notice that there is no debris or garbage on the street. The street looks fairly clean, in fact. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So someone was picking up garage?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those of us who lived in these two buildings, when we had the time, when it got a bit quiet, then we would clean around the buildings. There was a lot of wood or things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So would it be correct to say that while things were not as they were before the war, during the period of demilitarisation there were some changes to make people a bit more comfortable? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but very few.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like the usher's assistance in showing the witness photograph number 2, also part of the Defence Exhibit D795?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: 725, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry, just a matter of the interpretation. The witness said [B/C/S spoken] and that was translated "yes, but very few." "Yes, but very little," is another possible translation and that would make more sense to the answer with, "Were there some changes?" "Yes, but very little," perhaps it's -- perhaps it's all right but it didn't seem the best interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Madam, have you been able to follow -- Madam Kolenovic, have you understood what Mr. Jones said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And so basically we are being asked to establish whether the correct word in English would be "few" or "little". What is your position on this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I understood the question well. She asked me whether the situation had changed in the streets when they came. I said very little.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That explains it. Thank you. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Along those lines, when you talk about the changes, did this also include getting food as a result of humanitarian assistance as well?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In very small quantities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. If you would look with me at the next photograph, number 2, this is a photograph that you testified about yesterday, indicating that the houses that we see -- well, I'll rephrase the question. In the photograph that we see, it appears as though there are piles of material, appears to be either debris or dirt, some -- some -- something that was probably some form of substance that was taken from the buildings. Is that what we are looking at, the piles that you see?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those are houses that burned in early 1992, in April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who it was that placed these piles outside the buildings, these piles that we see, do we, in front of the building?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure, but I think it was a Swedish organisation that repaired the roofs on some of these houses later, and that's where the refugees lived later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the picture also depicts a truck. Do you see that to the right?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this truck, did you see this truck during 1992? And 1993, early part?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never, no. No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this would not be the truck that you told us that you saw during that period?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the period of 1992, did you -- were there any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. Richardson. I notice that both on this -- the number plate on this truck and on the previous truck, the first section is ZV. I don't know how the system was at the time in Bosnia but when you see a truck with a number plate which starts with the letters ZV, does that indicate anything to you? Does it indicate where that truck is registered? For example, does it mean that it is a truck from Zvornik or, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My car had a licence plate TZ. That's Tuzla. Perhaps for the municipality. Yes. Many cars before the war that had a -- town licence plates. The car that I had, my own car, had licence plates with the letters TZ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also testified that there were very few vehicles in Srebrenica during the war. Would that be correct? You just testified to a truck that you saw.

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any cars?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So absolutely no cars were operational in 1992, that you saw?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When the Serbs were there, I did see them. This was in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in early 1993, did you happen to see a black Mercedes in Srebrenica, at around the time General Morillon was present?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that period of time when Mr. Morillon was there, there were trucks that were -- that belonged to UNPROFOR perhaps or the humanitarian organisation?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When Morillon was there, there were many around the post office, but I don't know if these were military vehicles, UN vehicles. I don't understand. There were many around the post office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in that period of time, early 1993, did you see cars other than -- well, did you see cars, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When Morillon came, there were a number of vehicles. I don't know if they were military vehicles or not. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to take you to another topic, ask a series of questions about the refugees that came into Srebrenica. You testified that thousands of them arrived at different points during 1992 and in 1993. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And many of them you didn't know, I take it, as you testified before?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know any -- any of the refugees from before the war. I met some who were living close to me in the building, but otherwise there were too many of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You stated -- testified yesterday that you spoke with people from Bratunac, refugees, and you learned that they were -- there were a number of family members that were missing?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of course these people were very concerned about their family members, would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know if they took any actions in terms of contacting their family members or trying to locate them?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean? I don't understand. They were not able to return to their places of residence any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. I'll rephrase the question in fact. Were you aware that people from Bratunac were able to locate their family members via means of radio communication in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Information was -- different kinds of information was disseminated. Many of them went to the Vuk Karadzic school. A lot of them came to Srebrenica and then they came and they said that many men and women were detained at the Vuk Karadzic school. They came with different stories.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time that they were in Srebrenica itself, did you learn that they ventured to the PTT building or any other part of Srebrenica where they could make contact with family members to learn what their fate was, what had happened to them? Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That wasn't so in the beginning. There were no links or communications in the beginning. This was later, perhaps in late 1992, that there was a link established. I'm not exactly sure when that was but for a few months, I don't know exactly for how long, perhaps it was seven, eight months or six months, people didn't know anything. Many arrived who were living in my building and they said that they had seen their relatives who were killed. There were two or three girls who were separated from their families and only one of them was of age. There was also a grandmother who came with two small grandchildren, and they were just a few years old. She didn't know where her son and daughter-in-law were. There were hundreds of stories like that. I know only about what was going on in my building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just stop you for a moment because we do have to -- I do want to finish your cross-examination today, so if you will keep your answers as brief as possible. What I'm seeking from you is whether you were aware that a radio system existed in Srebrenica in 1992 where people could contact family members, find out what happened to them. If you could give me a simple yes or no to that question.

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I knew -- well, in 1993, I didn't know what was going on in the post office, during those two or three months, but when I threw my children on to those trucks, for six months I didn't know anything about my children. I didn't know where they were, if they it were alive or not, and then I went to the post office and I tried to find out something, some information about my children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were aware that there was some communication taking place in the post office, communication means, in other words?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1993, I saw that device when I went to see Ibrahim, oh, and again now I cannot remember his last name. It was something like this. It was a black thing. I don't understand these radio communications. It was a kind of black box and it was like "hello, hello," I've -- I don't really understand much about how it all works.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you perhaps see Ibrahim Becirevic?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Becirevic, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you went into this PTT building, was that the first time you had been there?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When Morillon was there, I was there every day, in front, with the children. There were thousands of us there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And prior to that occasion, were you there before, during 1992?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I was there in front of the post office when I fainted. I remember that well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if your husband visited that building in 1992 or 1993?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. He was near the hospital. I know for sure that he was near the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say he was near the hospital, what are you referring to? A building near the hospital?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
