utterances.text: No, no. In front of the hospital. He was there in front of the door on guard duty, because thousands of people would be trying to enter the hospital. They had to prevent them from going into the hospital in some way, and interfering with the wounded. There were a lot of problems there. Somebody had to secure the door. Suddenly you would have a thousand people trying to enter. It was a small hospital. There were many wounded and they would just be disturbing them for no reason. I mean, anyway, people were dying because of minor wounds and everybody wanted to go and visit their friends or relatives when they were in such a state.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour? Did you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wasn't quite clear in my mind when she was answering about the presence of her husband in that particular place, which occasion she was referring to, because I pretty much suspected that she still had in her mind the occasion when General Morillon was there and people were gathering in front of the PTT but please would -- could you address this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because I think we need to know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what period of time your husband stood on guard duty in front of the hospital? Was it in 1992? And 1993?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1993. He went in 1992, of course. Everybody went. I myself was there every day. Was also working there a lot. I mean there were people who were seriously wounded, dying there. The whole family would go there and friends and I also tried in my own way to contribute to calming the situation. It was a terrible situation. You would have thousands of people trying to enter through one door. I mean, we had problems amongst ourselves. You couldn't explain to anybody anything and nobody was listening to you anyway. The situation was terrible. All of us, the citizens, tried to help as much as we could and the refugees did as well. We wanted to be good, but it was something that was stronger than us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall what month it was -- when you testified that your husband was on guard duty in 1993, do you recall what period of time in 1993? Was it the early part, prior to General Morillon's arrival?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in early 1993, before Morillon arrived and afterwards as well. I was at the hospital myself every day. I was helping. I was taking sheets and bandages to the river to wash them, that we, the women, brought to the hospital from our own houses in the first place in order to help the wounded. I mean, it would be -- it's natural for people to want to do that anyway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you worked in the hospital, who was it that told you what you needed to do?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody told me anything. I did that on my own. Nobody paid attention to me. They saw that I was doing something useful, that I was taking cauldrons to the river to wash them, that I was helping the wounded, giving them water, that at least I was talking to them. I even -- there were some places where I couldn't go. There were a lot of wounds that were rotting. There were maggots in them so for me that was something that was difficult.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there other women like yourself also assisting at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I helped many girls, many girls -- I mean many were helping, women, girls, they were bringing water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this was in 1992 as well as early 1993?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to return to the topic of your husband, when he was on guard duty. Prior to your husband taking up guard duty in early 1993, was there someone else before him who was on guard duty as well? I mean before that time period that he was there. Back in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was always a bunch of people, men and women, in front of the doors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you testified -- and I'm asking not about the bunch of people but specifically with respect to the guard aspect of the hospital because you said that it was pretty chaotic. My question is: Was there a guard placed at the hospital in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. No. He just went there, and other men went and other women went. Simply to calm things down and prevent people from getting in, in large groups, but maybe three, five, ten at the time at most. We got organised amongst ourselves in order to do that -- in order to make it easier for the wounded upstairs, so as to prevent 2.000 to 3.000 people crowding into that small hospital. There were girls, young girls helping out as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. Richardson. Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry, it's just one thing which does occur occasionally, this witness was being asked the question and having been -- after Ms. Richardson said -- it's no criticism of Ms Richardson, but it's the way the interpretation came out. You said there, "It was pretty chaotic." Witness replied, "Yes." "My question is was there a guard placed at the hospital," and we could hear at that point the interpretation continuing and then she said, "No." It's unfortunate in the transcript you have yes, no, as if she is giving a confused answer I heard very clearly she said yes to the first part and no to the actual question. I just thought I should point that out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you agree to that, Ms. Richardson?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed. I thank you both and let's proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Getting back to the 1992 period and we are talking about the chaotic situation at the hospital, you said that there were other men there, we are talking about other men other than your husband; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So these people would change from time to time?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't actually organised. It was all spontaneous.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand, but they would change, the same person wouldn't be the person -- for instance if someone sat there during the day, that person wouldn't be there for two days at a stretch. That's what I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There wasn't just one person there. There were thousands of people in front of the doors, and my husband, since my apartment building is next door to the hospital, he was there every day and I myself was there almost every day. When he was home he would just go to the hospital because it was only humane to help out. Not just I myself and my husband. We all did that. I don't know how to explain that any better.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But let's -- let me ask you this: When he stood in front of the hospital, what did he do?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did go into the hospital. He would help the wounded. He would come out of the hospital, go home, and then go back. Sometimes he would go home to get something that he could take to the hospital, perhaps a sheet or a cloth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And did he -- did he prevent people from going in because the situation was chaotic? Was that one of the things that he did?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Everybody used to say that, that people should not go in in large groups, that they should go in in smaller groups because there were people waiting even up in the hills above the hospital, 2.000 to 3.000 were crowding to get in at any one time. I just can't explain to you the sort of situation that we were in. All of a sudden, you have more than 200 wounded and perhaps 50 to 60 dead and the entire population comes along and there is almost an assault at the hospital and it's even worse then than the damage that had been caused by the enemy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Now, you mention guard duty. Who was it that told him to be in the hospital performing these tasks that you just stated?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The witness didn't mention guard duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, initially --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: But that's not a word that I myself -- I'm just repeating what had been said earlier. I can rephrase the question, it's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please rephrase it it's easy to rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When your husband stood outside the hospital to prevent people from coming in and establish some kind of order, who was it, if you know, who told him to do this?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did it of his own accord. I hope you understand. It was a humane gesture on the part of the population. We wanted to help those who were hospitalised. And we wanted to prevent large crowds coming in. Let me reiterate this once again. We didn't want 1.000 people to enter the hospital at any one time altogether. Nobody ordered him anything. Nobody was in a position to order anyone anything. I mean, he was not really in a position to prevent 100 people pressing to enter either. He would have been completely unable to do so. They would have walked all over him. I mean he just did what he could. And people who were -- who had their relatives in hospital, especially young people -- children, young girls, you can't stop parents going into check on their children. And there were hundreds of those cases in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, you said that the situation was chaotic and he was there to help. Did he actually succeed in -- succeed in assisting and preventing too many people from going in, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Sometimes he helped people who had to go into the hospital, who would -- he would tell them, okay, right, you will be able to go in in a little while but he wasn't an actual guard on any duty. He was just a common citizen like they were. My child was in the hospital. My child had been wounded as well. We just wanted to calm things down in order to make it easier for the injured, for the wounded, in order for those two or three doctors to be able to do their job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move to something else.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you similarly to what I asked you initially about people in Srebrenica. I'd like to ask you about a series of people and just tell me if you know them or not. First person is Harudin Avdic. Hajrudin Avdic. Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It doesn't ring a bell. Perhaps I might have come across him but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Resid Efendic?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rasid Efendic sounds familiar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Hamdija Fezic?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a long-time Srebrenica resident?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can tell you the truth now to the extent that you're going to believe me. He married the daughter of a neighbour of mine, and sadly she died. He got married during the war. So I did know Hamdija Fezic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You knew him and saw him during the war?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. She would come as his wife used to live on the same floor in my building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if he had any particular duties in Srebrenica during the war, 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How could I know? I think he was a commander or something. That's what people used to say. But I never asked him. We didn't meet very often.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And what about Becir Begilovic?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bogilovic, you mean? No, I don't know the name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that a War Presidency had been established in Srebrenica during 1992 and also in 1993?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Perhaps after demilitarisation. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified that -- just getting back to the topic of the refugees and you said that a couple of them or a number of them had remained in your apartment and correct me if I misstate what you indicated yesterday, and you said that they stayed in your apartment for a short time, approximately five to six days. Do you recall that portion of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. There were people from Orlica, they were Roma.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they left your apartment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I tried to persuade them to do so. I said it was my apartment and that they should go, and some of them stayed behind. And I always had someone staying with us during the war, because we had too much space considering that other people were sleeping in the streets, sleeping rough in sheds, where there were leeks and everything so there were refugees in my flat as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The refugees not only in your flat but the refugees who came in they were housed into empty apartments and houses in Srebrenica during the period of 1992? Following the war? I should say after April of 1992.

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was anyone -- did anyone that you know of make arrangements for them to be housed in these different apartments?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Like me, I said to them to perhaps leave my apartment and go and look for something somewhere else because there were some business premises which stood empty. But there wasn't much in Srebrenica. There were some burnt down houses and they would stay there or just simply sleep rough in the streets. They used to sleep and cook and live in the streets. They would just put a blanket on the asphalt road and then sleep there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any person in particular that you know of in Srebrenica who would help the refugees find locations, where there was apartments, empty buildings, or any other type of accommodation, that assisted them?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That sort of organisation was simply impossible in Srebrenica. There were no preconditions for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also testified that you didn't go to the police.

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at the time that you had this problem with the refugees, did you know where -- I'm assuming you knew where the police station was.

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew where it was because I worked in the vicinity for years and I went past it every day but as to police, I don't know why you're asking me whether I ever went to the police. I don't know. I mean, I don't know of any police being operational during the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well my question -- if you will permit me so that it's clear to you, I'm asking whether or not when you had this problem if you went down to the police station where you knew it to be at the time, to complain to anyone that you were having this problem. I think you can answer that with a simple yes or no. That's all I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At what police station and what period of time do you have in mind, before the war?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm talking about the period of time when the refugees came to your apartment. You testified yesterday that you did not go to the police to complain about them barging into our apartment. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no one I could have complained to. Nothing was functioning anymore. There was just a -- common citizens there who had been driven out of their homes. I had nowhere to go and complain. Nobody to complain to. I suppose that's your job to ask questions but I find these questions very insulting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't mean to insult you. I'm just seeking to find out what action if any did you take. That's all. And some of these questions of course may seem quite obvious and insulting, but I'm simply seeking to see what it is that you did and what existed at the time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, and I have to support Madam Richardson in this, Madam Kolenovic. She's doing her duty here and although some questions might not appear exactly what you would like to hear, unless there is a serious and justifiable reason why I should not -- we should not allow it, we have to allow it and you need to answer it. So it's a harmless, innocent question which by no means we see as offensive. So -- on the other hand, I think she made the position clear enough yesterday and I don't think you should labour it much further.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, which is why I just suggested a yes or no answer -- do you need a few minutes, Ms. Kolenovic? We can have a short break, if you would like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Kolenovic, would you like a break or shall we continue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: A break, you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll have 25-minute break now and then we continue until we finish.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was actually going to suggest maybe -- it depends on how much time the witness wants but if Your Honour would like to do it that way, I have no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How much time -- Madam Kolenovic, look at me, please. How much time do you think you need?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Five or six minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So we'll have a short break of five or six minutes and then we continue. --- Break taken at 11.48 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's continue, Ms. Richardson. Are you okay now, Madam Kolenovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm okay.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Kolenovic, do you recall when it was that humanitarian aid first arrived in Srebrenica, either in 1992 or 1993?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall if in November of 1992 aid came to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to -- at this moment, Your Honour, to show a clip to the witness. I believe it's in Sanction. Just a moment, Your Honour, I'm trying to determine what the exhibit number is. Exhibit number 517. Your Honour, if we can have the booth give us some volume on the video. We would appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Kolenovic, if you could take a look at this tape that is being played.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you, do you recognise anyone in that -- in the video? There are two men. Do you recognise either one of them?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I only recognise one person but that was earlier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Perhaps we can go back and you can tell us who it was that you recognised in the photo -- in the video.

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This young man here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is his name? Who is he?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's Zele from Kazani.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop there. For the record, we are at 04 minutes and 1 second, 01.0. And I take it, Madam Kolenovic, that you are indicating the young man looking at us in the middle.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Yes, thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We can play the video a little bit more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise anyone there? Perhaps we can go back a bit. Is that person familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which? I think there are more than one person. If you're referring to the one in the foreground you need to be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, indeed I will. It's the person that's not foreground of the photograph. We are at 4170. If you don't, we can play it some more and if the image appears again, you can let us know if you recognise who that is so we can continue playing. Do you recognise the person?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who is that?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once at the hospital, I saw the person, but not actually all of him. Naser. And I also recognise Hamdija Fezic there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And where is Hamdija Fezic? Is that the person standing in the back?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the back or behind him?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In -- behind.

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. He's there. Maybe he was there before. He's not in the background. He's in the middle of the shot. I said that I knew Hamdija so I would like to show you which one is Hamdija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Can I ask whoever is moving the arrow there to point that arrow to the person who appears immediately behind the person who is in the foreground? That one. Now, you see that white arrow. Is that the person you're describing to us as Hamdija Fezic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it that one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Looks like Zele but Hamdija Fezic was there a little bit before. He had a beard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. We have to move back a little bit. So --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's Hamdija Fezic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right so we are at 414.1, and the -- in other words, it's the person that the arrow is pointing to? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the witness indicates it's Hamdija Fezic, the bearded gentleman who appears at the top left corner of -- or side of the picture.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Perhaps we can play some more of the video.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise the person who is standing in the background of the picture with -- holding something? It could be a weapon, something slender and black. Do you recognise that person?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, we are at 4 minutes 32 seconds point 9. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just if we can go back just a bit -- in the video, if we could just go forward one. If you take a look at this shot of the video, you see men, they appear to be in a line where -- for the record, we are at 4576. If you look at the way they are dressed, it appears as they have green camouflage uniforms on. Did you during 1992 and 1993 see any individuals dressed similarly in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I just object to the characterisation of the record as they, i.e. as in all the people in the line being in camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: They are not. I suggest that you direct the witness only to those who are according to you wearing camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Perfectly fair comment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would direct you to the individuals -- only those who appear to be wearing camouflage uniform. There is someone in the picture, from where I'm standing it appears to be a green brighter colour but it's not the same as the others. So perhaps you can tell us if -- and I'm speaking specifically with respect to the individuals who are what appears to be wearing camouflage uniforms. Did you see those type of uniforms in Srebrenica in 1992 and in 1993?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps we can play --

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw when Nurif and my brother-in-law came from Tuzla, they came and they all had uniforms. That group that came from Tuzla, all of them wore uniforms, including my brother-in-law Bekir Smajlovic. They all wore uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you just refresh our memory as to what month that was in 1992, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't winter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all I'll play of this portion of the video.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this scene look familiar to you? This was a video from November 1992. Was this -- the scene that I'm describing what you observed on the video, the UN trucks in the background, men in uniform, Naser Oric and the other individuals you pointed out, do you recall being present?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there when Morillon was there. There were several thousand of us. I was always there. We were asking for help. I was always moving between the hospital, my apartment building, the post office building. That's where I was most of the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And General Morillon was there in 1993?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm specifically asking is with respect to the picture, the video you just saw, which was taken in 1992, do you recall being present or even hearing about UN trucks being present in Srebrenica in November of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Morillon came, then that's when the UN trucks were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you don't remember a time before General Morillon being there that you had seen UN trucks or hearing about food being distributed in Srebrenica, in November of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. There was something that they had gone through Sase. It was snow. Snowing. I don't know whether this was 1992 or 1993 but I know, and I assert that we started to receive humanitarian food in 1993. That's when I saw the trucks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was one convoy, maybe it was 1992 to 1993. I really am not certain but it came through Sase. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just a small point. But it's perhaps a significant one. For P517, I just want to make clear that the Defence doesn't accept that this was these shots were taken in November 1992. Yes, it may say that on the video but without a witness to come here and say that he had set the timer on his video, we don't accept that those pictures were necessarily taken then. So it's -- just to let you know that that's in dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. It's important to know. Yes. Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall receiving food in November or December of 1992 that was perhaps from the humanitarian aid? And again this is before General Morillon was actually present.

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. You testified that your husband was a fighter and he belonged to a unit. Now, I'd like to ask you a series of questions about that. First of all, did your husband live with you the entire time of 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there days that he was not present -- when I say days, did he -- was he at the apartment every day or were there days at a time when he was not present?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was there every day. Sometimes he wasn't there. Sometimes I wasn't at home for two or three days, when I would go somewhere to get food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it the same with him, that he wouldn't be there for two or three days at a time?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did your husband receive food from the other fighters or any -- any other bodies in Srebrenica? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had no one to get the food from. He went to get food for himself. I'm not saying that anyone was a fighter. There was another side to it also. Actually, we were all fighters. Children were fighters. Men too. In such a situation, we were all major fighters, to be able to survive, to stay alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like you to concentrate on your husband because that's the series of questions that I'd like to ask you about. So if you would just bear with me, I'm just talking about your husband. Now, you assisted him in preparing for actions by making strips of cloth that he, you testified yesterday -- said could be used as bandages; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that you also gave the same strips of cloth to other individuals, other fighters, as well?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's say that they are fighters. Everything that I could do to help the population, I helped. Anything that I had in my house I would give as help. It was all a question of bare survival. My husband would go. I mean, he didn't even know where he was going. There was no destination. He didn't know where he was going. There is no Serb or Muslim village where my husband didn't go in order to find food. We had the misfortune that sometimes wherever we went we couldn't find anything. This was a rare thing for us. Perhaps we would find one meal or something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me just stop you there. Did your husband tell you he didn't know where he was going? Or is that an assumption you're making?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, it was normal that he didn't know where he was going. If there was shooting from Sase, it would be a powerful attack. At one time they practically entered the town. It was terrible. We all fled, all of the population went in the direction of Suceska. We almost practically all of us left Srebrenica because it was such a powerful attack, there was artillery, well, I don't know; I don't understand much about weapons. And my husband and all the other men went towards the woods up there. I don't know. I mean, I don't think that they could have held back such a powerful force, but they went any way. They had to go. Nobody ordered him, that he had to go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You -- were you present when he was with other members of his unit, including the person who was either the commander of the unit or who he reported to?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that he was in a group that was under the command of Mido. I don't know who Mido was. I never saw him in my life. Maybe sometimes I saw him in passing in Srebrenica but please believe me, my husband never told me, "That's the person."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, when -- the purpose of your husband going on these actions was to get food?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he brought food back with him?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said very rarely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how often would he go on these actions to get food? And I'm talking specifically about 1992 into early 1993.

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, the entire population of Srebrenica was on the move. There was no Muslim village --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just stop you for a moment because I do want to finish your testimony today. So if you could just perhaps assist me by answering only the question that I'm asking, I think we can get through what it is that I need to know. How often did your husband - only your husband - go out on actions for food? Did he go on a monthly basis, beginning in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every day, he would either be going to the woods to bring back wood, which he would cut up and bring up to the sixth floor or he would go to get water or he would go somewhere to bring back food, to look for food. When it was spring he had to go to the woods to bring back leaves so that the children could eat. He would bring back some grass from the soil that was edible so that we could eat. He just went everywhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But there were times that he went on actions, not to the woods to bring back leaves. There were times that he actually went out on actions with other fighters.

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wherever he went in the actions, I was there as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go with him during the -- did you go together?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not together with him but in the same direction. Perhaps taking a different road. Some five to six thousand, maybe up to 10.000 of us would go. I mean nobody could count us. We knew, all of the population, that this was our own source of food, whether we are talking about Muslim villages or Serb villages, I would go and rob and grab food from Muslim villages also to bring back something so that my children could survive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your husband -- you said you would follow him. So that means he went first; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't follow him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did he --

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we were going to Sase, the whole population would go. Only those who couldn't walk wouldn't go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question --

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would be going in one direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Your husband didn't go with you; is that correct? You just testified that you didn't go together.

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't follow him. I didn't go behind him, but I went in the same direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he go into these actions or these Serb villages first, before you did?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Civilians would enter before the soldiers would, into the villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there ever a time that you entered before the fighters? And which village was that?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was trying to get in but since there were many people that were more able than myself, I was never among the first, but we went in en masse. We didn't know who was civilian, who was soldier. Nothing was known.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So as far as you know, when you got to the village, the fighters could have been there already. You don't know.

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that but we went in en masse. A few thousand of us. How could I tell who was soldier and who wasn't?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry, it's actually the second time that the interpretation that borci [phoen] has come out as "soldier." In the past borci has been "fighter."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, in fact I was wondering, but I didn't see you stand up.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We checked and it's borci twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So borci is --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: "Fighter," and vojnici is "soldier."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You agree to that, Ms. Richardson?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. [Microphone not activated]. Pardon me. If I could just speak with my colleagues for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, let me just say this. I think we've had testimony in the past about people calling individuals with weapons soldiers. Now if we are referring specifically to this witness and what she said, then I have no problems with respect to what translation is being given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Let's go ahead. I take it that she used the word which should have been interpreted as fighters and not soldiers. That's it. Let's move. Or let's proceed, anyway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to read from a portion of your testimony yesterday, so if you could listen carefully and I'd ask you to comment on it. Page 56 of the transcript. "Okay." Question: "Okay, now I want to ask you about your family members on that day. First of all your husband. Was he with you on the 7th of January or was he elsewhere?" "No. He wasn't with me." "Do you know where he was on the 7th of January?" "He was in Kravica." "Did he tell you anything about what he saw or observed on that day?" "He did." "What did he tell you briefly?" Answer: "He criticised the civilians. In fact, he said why did they have to create so much chaos in Kravica? They entered and I myself would do that whenever I was looking for food, in order to frighten the Serbs and get them to leave their houses, let's say five or six or 10.000 of us would enter the village but I can guarantee that in Kravica, well, perhaps 5.000 could have gone to Kravica. The entire population of Srebrenica must have been in Kravica on that day. It is unspeakable. I mean, it's like some kind of film. People were crying, screaming, banging pots. They were driven in a way that was totally frightening." I'd like to bring you back to the portion where you said your husband criticised the civilians. Based on what you said yesterday, clearly there is a difference between the civilians and people who considered themselves fighters such as your husband. You agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And with respect to Kravica, your husband was there before you. He was there on the 7th. And I believe you testified you got there on the 8th.

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And with respect to Bjelovac, your husband was in Bjelovac before you got there. Is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I wasn't in Bjelovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But your husband was?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And with respect to Fakovici, was your husband also in Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was he?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there any reason that he did not go to Fakovici on the day that thousands of the population went?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somebody always had to stay behind to watch the house. Otherwise it would be emptied. Sometimes we would take a risk but on occasion we would leave someone behind, and, for example, when we went to Kravica, I left the children behind. But they went out nonetheless. There was no way to control anyone in Srebrenica. I couldn't protect my own house, my own doorstep.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you went out looking for food while your husband stayed behind to watch the house?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He remained behind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was a fighter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you want her to answer this question or is it just a remark.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I'll withdraw the question as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, he was a fighter and he stayed at home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he believe you more capable of gathering food than he was? Is that why you went out and he did not?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He couldn't prevent me from going.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did he -- if you didn't go that day, and he didn't go that day, how were you expected to eat, if you had no food?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think you need to -- don't answer that question. That's why she went.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wherever my husband wanted to go, he went of his own accord. He could stay at home whenever he wanted to. He could leave when he felt the need to.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Just a moment, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sticking with that portion of your testimony that I read to you yesterday, where you described that you yourself -- well, withdraw that. Let me just ask you about the preparation for the civilians going out. Now, you testified that thousands of civilians would go out to the Serb villages seeking food?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they would do this and go to the areas that the fighters were in. Would that be a correct assessment?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they would go out -- how did you know -- I'll rephrase. How did you yourself and the thousands of other civilians know which Serb village to go to on that particular day?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were people from nine municipalities, and we knew where the Serb villages were around Srebrenica, and that was the only source of food and the only way for us to survive. As soon as we -- we would get humanitarian aid we would stay and get -- go no where.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the question is: How did you yourself know -- you -- how did you know what village, what Serb village to go to? For instance, by way of example, you went to Sase. How did you know to go to Sase?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be widely known in a couple of days or it would be known 15 days or a month before and we would know that the Serbs were in Sase, they were attacking from there and there is food there. So we have to go. And I would -- I was the first to excerpt some pressure on my husband, telling him go to that Serb village, bring something back. If you are not going, I am. I have to feed my children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who decided what day you would actually go? The thousands of people in search of food. Who decided the exact day?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire town, the entire population exerted pressure and we, the women, organised ourselves to go and we discussed this amongst ourselves. Even children discussed that. There is this village of Kravica, there is a lot of food there. It would suffice for someone to say --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I hate to interrupt you and I appreciate the information but I'm seeking to get what is basically a very simple question, which is who decided what day? Now, you said the women would gather together to prepare, but who decided the day that you would go? I see Mr. Jones is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I object to the question because Ms. Richardson is saying it's a very simple question, but it carries with it all sorts of assumptions that there is one person who decided when everyone would go, that all of the down to the man, woman, and child, the thousands of them, would all follow that decision, and that this witness knows about that. Perhaps it's a question of foundation but it's just a total shot in the dark who told thousands of people to go somewhere on the certain day. And it's no wonder if the witness doesn't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you, Mr. Jones. Ms. Richardson, Could you rephrase the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, I can do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think if you direct it -- it's -- it can be approached in very simple terms because I don't -- I don't -- I'm not surprised that she has not answered your question because it wasn't, I think, as clear or --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I'll do my best, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Kolenovic, I'll rephrase the question. You went to Kravica, I believe you said on the 8th. And you testified that the -- your husband was there on the 7th. I am simply seeking an answer from you about whom it was that decided, as far as you know, that the 7th of January would be the day that everyone would go to Kravica.

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire population. It was the only and the last source of food for us to survive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you also said that there were preparations made. Could you tell us a little bit more about that? What kind of preparations did the women and some of the children make in preparation for actions such as Kravica or Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To reiterate, Kravica was the only source of food that we could use to survive. The entire population discussed this, not for days but for months, that Kravica is the only source that would enable us to survive. Had there been any food thrown from the air planes we wouldn't have gone to Kravica. Had we received anything before Kravica or 1992 had we received anything from the planes we would have stayed in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say the entire population discussed this, was there a town meeting, a vote taken, about attacking Kravica -- or execution me, conducting an action in Kravica on the 7th of January?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People simply discussed this, that we would go to Kravica to get food. No one discussed an attack. No one went there with an intent to attack Kravica and the people there. It was simply a source of food for us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, when you say no one went to Kravica with the intent of attacking, did you go to Kravica, and by you I mean the entire population, did you go to Kravica to ask the Serbs who were residing in Srebrenica for food? Is that what your testimony is? In a non-violent way?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who would give me that? If I were caught by a Serb they would slit my throat or they would kill me the way they were doing at the beginning. My best neighbours, the people I loved, were doing that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But my question is: And I'll ask you again. It was not the intention of the thousands of Muslims to go into Kravica, knock on the doors of the Serbs, and ask them to give you food. That was not the intention, was it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: She has already told you, Ms. Richardson, that it wasn't. And it couldn't be, actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to quote from yesterday's testimony, page 73.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Just a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to get back to the preparations that you undertook prior to going in search of food to the Serb villages, including Kravica and Sase or perhaps Bjelovac. Did you carry bags with you? Yourself and the thousands of others.

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the time that you decided to leave, would you gather together with people from your building and others in the town to leave at a particular time?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would join with a larger group of people. If it was at night or in the morning, whenever I went there, there were already thousands of people there before me. When -- wherever I went --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's correction, "whenever I went there was always someone there ahead of me."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you knew either people had gone before you so there were people going before you and then you yourself went at various times but there were always thousands of people at the time that you were present, ready to leave to go in search of food?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these were primarily women and children?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Women, children, men, the entire population was on the move. The only people that didn't were those who couldn't walk and, of course, very small children, babies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So that we are clear, though, your husband didn't set out with you at any particular point of these actions, together?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we went several times to Voljavica. We went there together, during the night, to take the food from the fields up to the Drina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you -- did your -- did you encounter any -- I'll rephrase the question. When you went to Voljavica with your husband, were there other people present?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. What do you mean present?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, were there thousands of people with you when you went to Voljavica, when you were with your husband?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were people of about 1, 2 or 300, and we would go into the fields, but it was always done during the night. We couldn't do that during the day because the Serbs could see it all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you went to Fakovici, do you recall when that was?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was the end of the fall or beginning of the winter, maybe in October.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And when you went, do you remember what time of day you set out to go to Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was at night. I don't know the date. It's not close by. It was several kilometres away. It would take one, seven, eight hours to reach there and then you would have to hide because there were shells falling from all sides and one would get tired as well. You had to rest. And on occasion I would be absent for three days without coming back home, and then sometimes we would go astray. There was shooting. We couldn't go back immediately and we would have to stay in the forest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And thousands of people would stay in the forest, correct?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there came a point in time that the people left the forest and they would go into either the town of Fakovici itself or surrounding villages?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We moved everywhere. To Fakovici and the surrounding villages, and in the forests, the fields.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But there came a point after you gathered together in the forest that you actually went into the town. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What town?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'll rephrase it. We are talking --

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see any other town apart from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let me rephrase my question. I may be confusing you actually. We are talking about Fakovici at the moment and you said that you -- that you went with thousands of people with the intent to go to Fakovici, which is a Serb village, correct?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't in Fakovici. I tried to get there but I was never in Fakovici. And I saw thousands of people moving, some wounded, some were departing, some coming back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe you testified about that yesterday so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But she also said that she never entered Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in your attempt to get to Fakovici --

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you attempted to get to Fakovici. Now --

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- let's talk about your going to Bjelovac. Was -- do you recall that time?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in fact you didn't go to Bjelovac but you actually went to Sase; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct. I started towards Bjelovac but I didn't go further than Sase. I went -- the intent to reach Bjelovac but I went as far as Sase, and not further.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your husband already in -- he went to Bjelovac, correct?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he leave the house before you did?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time did you leave?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right after him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time did he leave?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How can I know? I didn't look at my watch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was dark. Whether it was dusk or night, I don't know. It was dark.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you -- had you been to Bjelovac before?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so -- and this is with respect to Fakovici, had you been to Fakovici before? Did you know the path to go to, to get to Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you went along with thousands of others who knew the way to both Bjelovac and Fakovici, would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know whether they knew. I went together with a lot of other people, wherever they went I went along.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's with people like yourself, some of them you knew, would that be a correct assessment?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course some knew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when the civilians went to Bjelovac, and this is with respect only to Bjelovac, do you recall whether some of them were wearing sheets over their clothing?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My husband also carried a sheet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, wore a sheet.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was tied in a knot here. It was winter. They had to survive, and even I had a sheet. It was so cold. And during day light, one could see other people -- other people easier, but it was different, and easier in the night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you wore the sheet to prevent people from seeing you?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, with respect to Kravica, was the preparation conducted in a similar manner, that you collected your bags and you and thousands of others set out to go to Kravica?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your husband left the day before, would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I went on the 7th as well but I wasn't in Kravica on the 7th, and I left the children behind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you set out on the 7th with the intent to get to Kravica on the 7th? Was that the plan?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, however, you ended up spending the night so you actually entered Kravica on the 8th, the next day?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you entered Kravica, you testified that there were men, perhaps fighters, there, with weapons preventing you and others from going into Kravica. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why it was they were trying to prevent you from going into Kravica to get food?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, we were all like vultures, hungry vultures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that but why did they prevent you from going to get food? What was their purpose? They didn't want you to eat?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. They wanted us to eat, but they were afraid that we would get, all of us, killed there. There was a lot of shooting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they weren't preventing you from going in for food but for your safety?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as -- you testified as well that when you went into -- when you yourself -- you testified, entered the village -- I'll rephrase the question. You talked about -- you testified about the fact that your husband had criticised the civilians and he -- we were -- I think the time you were testifying, you were referring to the Kravica action. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't say that my husband criticised the civilians. He criticised me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Because yesterday, in the transcript, you -- you were asked about --

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see my husband there in Kravica, but only when we came back home, and he criticised me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Because what you testified yesterday, unless there is a problem with the transcript, that he criticised the civilians and said "they have created so much chaos in Kravica." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not my husband, not just my husband. Everybody criticised the civilians. My husband criticised me, and perhaps all of those who were in our building, that there was a lot of chaos created once we entered Kravica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, part of the -- pardon me, would you like to continue?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And I also said that some armed people who had several rifles stopped us and tried to apply force against us civilians, trying to stop us from going to Kravica. That's what I saw, and that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you testified that civilians would scream and bang pots as they would enter the Serb villages. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... this was done so that you can frighten the Serbs and get them to leave their houses?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this was done after the fighters had already entered the Serb villages, ahead of you?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I don't recall the witness saying that could we have a reference to the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Could we have reference to the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It does sound, it does sound very much as if this is evidence --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: She never said that. But if you want to ask the question, of course you're free to ask.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour it was question, and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers not overlap, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Whether it's banging on pots and pans occurred before the fighters entered the village or after or during, I mean what --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I can take it in step by step.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But she never said -- gave an indication.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, and Ms. Kolenovic, so that you don't misunderstand me, I never said that you said that it was a question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So perhaps we could take it one step at a time. When civilians entered the villages, they would scream and bang pots. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the civilians would usually enter the villages after the fighters were already engaged in fighting. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The civilians would go in when the fighters were there, too. They would go in together. I think I said that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, when you say go in together, let's make sure that that's clear. When you yourself went in, let's say for instance Kravica, your husband was not present on the 8th, when you went in, with you, side by side.

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the same is true for Bjelovac, correct? Sase. When you went into Sase, your husband wasn't with you side by side, correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: She never made it to Bjelovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I corrected it and said Sase, yes. Your Honour, I would just like to -- pardon me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, evidently the witness's answer is not on the transcript, to my last question. I believe I asked is it true for Bjelovac --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Put the question again. No problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question to you was whether or not your husband was with you side by side when you entered Sase.

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I assume we are going straight to 1.30?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please try to finish.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, I am; that's why I asked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified as well about taking sheets to make clothing for people such as the refugees who didn't have any.

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Richardson, before you continue, do you plan to have a re-examination, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I was going to ask Ms. Richardson to leave me enough time for my re-examination, about 15 minutes currently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So there is -- yes, Ms. Richardson. Do you think you can conclude in about ten minutes?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I'll try my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you can see we are all trying to work out the time so I can complete your cross-examination today so I would appreciate it if the answers are brief. Not to go back over what you testified to before, but you said you helped your husband prepare strips of material to be used as bandages in the event that he was injured?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd just like to show you a tape, if you will, and ask you a series of questions about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So at this time, Your Honour, the clip is presently on Sanction. Prosecution's Exhibit 329.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I just say one thing, Your Honour? My objections to the interview are on record. I'm sorry, I did have the reference for the date. We say that this is not -- this 12th of May, this year, we say that until a witness comes along and says, "Yes, this is an interview of Naser Oric properly conducted on this day," then it's nothing more than a purported interview and I just -- I won't object from now on. I wanted it to be on the record henceforth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do appreciate that, especially in the presence of the witness. Perhaps we can show this video now and if you could just look at the video and to what's being said on the video I'd like to ask you a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: "As we didn't have any logistics in terms of uniforms in the way that we would get our uniforms we would actually kill the Chetnik and take the uniform off and wear that. Most of us had Chetnik uniforms. So always there would then be very close fighting, which we always preferred to have close hand-to-hand fighting because we didn't have the ammunition to carry out a fire fight from a long distance away. So I went off -- so what we would do would be we would attach ribbons, so -- either around the head or else on the shoulder or on the -- around the arms, ribbon -- various coloured ribbons so that we would be able to recognise each other. We always tried to find an easily recognisable but unusual colour which people wouldn't be able to simply sort of look around and find something of that colour and tie it on themselves. So that they -- they, for example, would find some materials of the same colour, put this on and then -- then attack us, surprise us and then attack us in that way."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Having heard that bit of information about the use of ribbons, my question is: What you prepared for your husband in terms of strips of material, is it plausible that these were used as headbands or bands for the arms as was stated in the video, as identified -- as identification, for identification purposes?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps. How could I know? My husband told me that he needed those bands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Just one final question, Your Honour. I can conclude.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You stated that because of the lack of clothing that some people were able to use -- were able to sew white trousers made from the traditional Muslim dress. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not white trousers from the pantaloons, but they used white sheets to make the trousers. But they also used pantaloons to make trousers. Pantaloons were of a patterned fabric. I didn't see any women there wearing white pantaloons, the pantaloons were always patterned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, these trousers -- the sheets, were they made to look as though they were uniforms such as a full uniform, where there is a top, a jacket, and white pants as well, matching, to appear as though they were uniforms?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said yesterday that they used duvets to make them which were multi-coloured on one side and plain on the others, duvets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall if they were made to appear as uniforms? Do you recall what they looked like?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I also had a very nice duvet, and I made one for myself, just so that I could have a kind of track suit.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have any further questions and I thank you, Madam Kolenovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you Ms. Richardson. Mr. Jones re-examination. Re-examined by Mr. Jones:

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Kolenovic I just have a few questions for you. First of all you identified today on the video you were shown, someone as Zele. Do you remember his full name?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I knew it. Zele -- I can't really say all that much, because when I was at my apartment, that was when they used a metal file to cut Zele's arm. He was a friend of mine from school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't want to -- you to be upset about it. Do you happen to know his name, his first and second name? That's all we need for the record. And then we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember his first and last name. All I know is that we used to call him Zele.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember what he did before the war, in terms of job or recreation?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I think that he was involved in music, and he lived in Kazani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what instrument he played?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he played the guitar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so -- I'm going to move very quickly, but do you remember when his arm was amputated?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'm moving on to a different area so we can leave Zele.
