You told us today your husband one point you said he was in a unit another point you said it wasn't really a unit. You also told us, and it's page 65, line 18, that nobody ordered him to go, nobody ordered your husband to go to one place or another. Firstly; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you referred to a Mido as his commander. Do I take it from that, when you said nobody ordered your husband, that Mido didn't order your husband either? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So the person you describe as his commander, your husband's commander, didn't in fact order him to do anything? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Again, the "no" was to the first part of the question, and the "it's correct" was to the second part, for the record. Now, you've been asked about the distinction between fighters and civilians. You also said, and it's page 64, lines 11 to 12, "Actually we were all fighters, children were fighters." Now, do you stand by that, that all of you, women and children in one sense were fighters?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in a certain sense. We really were all fighters. It was one enclave. I really cannot tell that to anyone else. Only those who were there know how it was. We were all fighters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So I take it from that that if you saw someone and you didn't know who they were, simply by looking at them you wouldn't say, "Oh, that's a fighter or that's not a fighter, he's in so and so's unit or he's in another unit." You simply wouldn't know based on someone's appearance what their status was? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I thank you. Now, you were also asked a lot today about whether civilians went into actions at the same time as fighters or afterwards. Page 67, lines 22, 23, I quote, you said, "Civilians would enter before the soldiers into the villages." Now, is that -- is that correct? Is that testimony correct? To your knowledge, civilians would -- would enter before soldiers or fighters or whichever term you used?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't have the opportunity to tell you that in more detail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well that's fine. I think that's sufficient detail for our purposes. Finally, you were asked today about these ribbons which you prepared for your husband. I want to ask firstly, in 1992, 1993, was your relationship with your husband one in which he was generally truthful with you or was he evasive? Was he -- what sort of relationship did you have with your husband?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He couldn't lie to me or to hide anything from me, or to lie to me and say something was not like that when I knew the whole situation, and I was in such a situation that you couldn't make anything up or conceal anything or do anything without us knowing about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, when you made these ribbons for your husband, what did you understand they were to be used for?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How should I know? He said that he needed to have that in his pocket in case he was wounded, to have it with him, because we have that in our experience. I mentioned Zele. Many people had their limbs cut off in order to staunch the blood. I mean he said that he needed these bands. I even carried some in my pocket.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And so when he said that to you, did you believe him?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Jones. Judge Brydensholt? Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: At the time that your husband assisted at the hospital, when he went there and sometimes I understand he was placed before the entrance to prevent a lot of people to go into the hospital, I understand that. Do you remember, on those occasions, did he bring the rifle he had got?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. A simple question, Madam. Are your children both alive? Your two sons?

utterances.speaker: SABRA  KOLENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank God, yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. That basically brings your testimony to an end now. Which means that we'll get the machinery in motion to facilitate your return back home to Sarajevo as quickly as possible. The airport is still closed over there, I take it. I don't know. But I'm sure that all the assistance will be forthcoming to facilitate your return back home as early as possible. On behalf of the Tribunal, and particularly on behalf of Judge Brydensholt, and also on behalf of Judge Eser who couldn't be with us today, and on my own behalf, I should like to thank you, Ms. Kolenovic, for having been kind enough to come forward and give evidence on these two days. I know it hasn't been easy, but unfortunately these things happen. As I said, you will be escorted now by our usher, and I'm sure that you will receive all assistance you require. On behalf of everyone present here, may I also wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we will be sitting now on Monday. Is it morning? Morning sitting. And do you know the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Courtroom III so we will continue Monday morning at 9.00 in Courtroom III. MR. DI FAZIO: Just one very brief matter, probably more a matter for the Defence. Your Honour mentioned -- asked the witness where she resided and she gave an address. I don't know if that causes her any consequences or if it's something we should consider redacting. I don't know, and I simply raise it -- it suddenly occurred to me as I saw it and I just mention it. I'm making no application.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's very kind of Mr. Di Fazio to mention it. I suppose out of an abundance of caution, if it's possible to redact her address, we should do it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's redact her address before we leave please and the place where she mentions where she is living, including the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Page 92, line 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You've spoken also with our legal officer with regard to the sitting of the 19th September, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course, we will approach that matter as we go along, simply everything depends on whether that will be possible or not. Because obviously if one witness lasts longer or we don't finish as planned, then we will revert back, all right? Thanks. So let me sign it, please. The important thing is that it is redacted. In other words, we have the advantage of the 30-minute delay. There is a problem with the printing, apparently, so I can't sign it now.
